title: Cloud Migration Planning: Readiness, Cutover, and Rollback
description: A practical cloud migration planning guide covering workload discovery, dependency mapping, migration strategy, data validation, cutover, security, rollback, and post-migration optimization.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Inventory Workloads and Dependencies
sections.body: Start with an inventory of applications, databases, scheduled jobs, storage, identities, network paths, external services, and operational owners. For each workload, record its business criticality, data sensitivity, dependencies, performance needs, recovery expectations, and current cost. Identify undocumented connections before moving anything. A service that appears independent may rely on a shared database, fixed IP address, file share, or scheduled task. This map is the foundation for sequencing and risk assessment.

sections.title: Choose a Migration Strategy Per Workload
sections.body: Some workloads can move with minimal code changes; others need redesign, replacement, or retirement. Choose a strategy based on the reason for migration, the system's lifecycle, and the value of changing its architecture. Avoid forcing every application into the same pattern. Record the expected benefit, engineering effort, risk, and post-migration operating model for each choice. If the business case depends on cost savings, include data transfer, managed service, observability, support, and staffing costs rather than comparing only compute prices.

sections.title: Prepare the Target Environment
sections.body: Before migrating a production workload, verify the target environment is ready.
items: Identity, roles, network boundaries, secrets, and encryption are configured.
Infrastructure changes are repeatable and reviewed through version control.
Backups and restore procedures have been tested.
Monitoring, alerting, logs, and ownership are in place.
Capacity, quotas, regional requirements, and data residency are understood.
Deployment and rollback paths are documented and rehearsed.
The team knows how to escalate incidents during the migration window.

sections.title: Plan Data Transfer and Validation
sections.body: Determine how data will be copied, synchronized, validated, and protected during the move. For large or changing datasets, decide how writes are handled while the source and target are not fully aligned. Validate record counts, checksums or suitable integrity checks, relationships, permissions, and application-level behavior. Test restore from the target backup rather than assuming a successful copy is enough. Document how the final synchronization will work and who has authority to declare the data ready for cutover.

sections.title: Rehearse Cutover and Rollback
sections.body: Create a runbook with the order of operations, communication plan, freeze window, DNS or routing changes, validation steps, go/no-go criteria, and named decision-makers. Define rollback triggers before the migration begins and confirm that the source remains usable until acceptance. Rehearse the process in a representative environment and record the time each step takes. Avoid relying on a rollback plan that assumes data written after cutover can be discarded without business impact; define how writes are reconciled if the team returns to the source.

sections.title: Secure and Observe the New Platform
sections.body: Review access permissions, secret storage, network exposure, patching, logging, backup retention, and incident response after migration. Confirm that monitoring captures the user journeys and dependencies that matter, and compare latency, errors, availability, and cost with the baseline. Ensure that alert routes and runbooks refer to the new environment. Remove obsolete credentials and temporary migration access. Migration changes the operational boundary, so update inventories, diagrams, recovery procedures, and ownership records.

sections.title: Optimize Only After Stabilization
sections.body: Do not combine a risky migration with broad optimization unless the scope and rollback plan justify it. First confirm functional correctness, reliability, security, and support readiness. Then review utilization, storage lifecycle, data transfer, reserved capacity, and managed-service choices against actual usage. Track cost by workload and owner so unexpected increases are visible. Document what improved, what regressed, and which assumptions in the migration plan were wrong. Use those findings to plan the next workload more accurately.
